# Published-release migration compatibility

`alpha-1.json` and `alpha-2.json` were independently generated by the published
`0.1.0-alpha.1` and `0.1.0-alpha.2` core, SQLite, Postgres, and MySQL artifacts.
Each records its immutable SHA-512 integrities,
rendered migration SQL, history metadata, model snapshots, and canonical
checksums. The migration is a representative synthetic application authored
for qualification; its source is held fixed in
[`historical-migration-contract.js`](../../../scripts/historical-migration-contract.js).

`npm run check:migration-compatibility` builds the candidate and compares its
reviewed original migration SQL and checksum with all three recorded provider
contracts. The original authored source and published fixture remain unchanged.
The stronger SQLite required-key DDL changes that original callback's digest:
the live upgrade first proves it is refused without changing history, then uses
[`preserve-historical-migration-sql.js`](../../../scripts/preserve-historical-migration-sql.js)
to pin the recorded SQL, parameters and transaction options. PostgreSQL and
MySQL callbacks retain their original digests. Alpha.2 already contains the
required-key repair and retains its authored digest on all three providers.
This is a reviewed application
upgrade procedure, not automatic compatibility for changed migration callbacks.
It compares the recorded format-v1 model snapshots semantically,
so compatible serialization additions do not become schema changes.

It then installs the exact historical package versions into a separate
consumer, verifies all four package integrities against this receipt, and
starts a process using that published release to create the database, write its migration history,
and save a versioned entity. The candidate reads and updates that entity,
recognizes the original migration without reapplying it, appends a new
migration, reruns it idempotently, and rolls it back. It verifies that the
original history row, checksum, release version, and application data survive.
Changing the body of an already applied migration is refused without rewriting
history. SQLite runs in the default gate; Postgres and MySQL run in their live
CI lanes.

Remote qualification requires `ENTITYKIT_COMPAT_DATABASE_URL` with a database
name containing `test`, `qualification`, or `hardening`. It owns and recreates
`entitykit_historical_books` and `__entitykit_migrations` in that isolated
database. Never run this qualification against application data.

```sh
npm run check:migration-compatibility
ENTITYKIT_COMPAT_DATABASE_URL=postgres://entitykit:entitykit@127.0.0.1:5432/entitykit_test \
  npm run check:migration-compatibility:postgres
ENTITYKIT_COMPAT_DATABASE_URL=mysql://root:entitykit@127.0.0.1:3306/entitykit_test \
  npm run check:migration-compatibility:mysql
```

The default campaign runs both baselines. Select one with a full release
version after the provider argument; a reused `ENTITYKIT_LEGACY_CONSUMER` also
requires that selector and must match the chosen receipt exactly.

Future releases add fixtures and retain prior fixtures and authored sources.
Install the four packages of the published baseline and the pinned test
drivers into a clean consumer, then run
`node scripts/record-migration-compatibility.js /absolute/consumer/path 0.1.0-alpha.N`
from the repository. The recorder requires npm-installed artifacts at that
exact version and refuses an existing destination. Review each new receipt;
never regenerate one using candidate packages to hide an incompatibility.
